subject: geography
title: Grid References
welcome_lead: Let's find places on a map! Master 4-figure and 6-figure grid references so you'll never be lost.
meta_desc: KS3 Geography adventure on 4-figure and 6-figure grid references.
final_note: Excellent! You can now read map grid references confidently.

concepts.def: Numbers that pinpoint a location on a map.
Horizontal grid line read going east.
Vertical grid line read going north.
Pinpoints a spot within a square.
Ordnance Survey map of the UK.

walkthroughs.h2: Along the corridor, up the stairs
walkthroughs.body_html: Always read eastings first, then northings. Remember: along the corridor, then up the stairs.
Take the easting at the bottom-left corner (e.g. 12) and the northing (e.g. 34). Together: 1234 refers to the whole square.
Imagine each square split into tenths. Read the extra digit for east (e.g. 5/10) then north (e.g. 7/10). Reference becomes 125347.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a hurricane and a tornado?
options: Hurricanes are huge (hundreds of km) tropical ocean storms that last days; tornadoes are small (tens of metres) intense rotating columns from thunderstorms over land, lasting minutes.
A tornado is just a small hurricane.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data in geography fieldwork?
options: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher (surveys, measurements, observations); secondary data already exists and is found in sources (census data, maps, published reports).
A tornado is just a small hurricane.
Primary data is collected in primary schools and secondary data in secondary schools.
Primary data is more important and secondary data is less reliable.
